Frisket now ships for 32-bit Windows: `frisket-0.10.0-win-x86-native.zip` holds the library for a Win32 program, and
`frisket-0.10.0-win-x86-cli.zip` the command line.

**Upgrade if you call the native library from a 32-bit Windows program.** Nothing else changes: the three NuGet
packages, the command line and the native library on every other target behave exactly as in 0.9.0, and their
documents are the same. Nothing was removed or renamed.

## Fixed: a 32-bit library crashed on its first call

`frisket.h` and every wrapper declare the entry points `cdecl`, while the library itself declared no calling
convention. On 64-bit Windows, ARM64 and Linux there is only one, so this changed nothing. On 32-bit Windows, .NET then
uses `stdcall`. A library built for x86 by hand popped each call's arguments, and the caller popped them again. A Win32
program crashed on its first call with an argument.

Every entry point now declares `cdecl`. The import library `frisket.lib` shows it: it names `_fk_render` and no longer
`_fk_render@24`, so a C or C++ program compiled against `frisket.h` links and runs.

## The 32-bit archive

| File | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `frisket.dll` | the library, built for x86 |
| `frisket.lib` | the import library, for a C or C++ program that links against it |
| `frisket.h` | the C interface |
| `wrappers/` | C++, Pascal and Python, unchanged from the other targets |

The Pascal wrapper now compiles with Delphi 10.4 as well as Free Pascal: it declares its own pointer where it used
`PInt32`, which Delphi 10.4 does not have. Delphi 5 cannot compile it. The wrapper uses records with methods and
`UTF8String`, which Delphi 5 does not have.

## Worth checking

- **If you made a 32-bit build work by declaring the imports `stdcall`**, declare them `cdecl` again, as `frisket.h`
  and the Pascal wrapper do. A `stdcall` declaration against this library fails the same way in reverse.

Every release now checks the x86 library on its own runner, as a 32-bit process. A 32-bit Python loads it, and with
the command line built for x86 and the managed command line it must write the same document. A 32-bit C program built
against the import library must link, run and write that document too. That last check is the one that fails if any
entry point loses `cdecl`.
